Taskmasters
TASK-mas-terz
noun (plural)
From task, through the Old French tasche and Late Latin tasca, “an imposed piece of work,” joined to master; rendering the Hebrew sar mas, “chief of the levy,” the officer set over forced labour to exact the appointed quota.

Biblical Definition

Taskmasters are the officers Pharaoh set over Israel to break them by labour: “Therefore they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens” (Exo 1:11). The word carries its own purpose in it — the task is not work but affliction, labour weaponized, the quota used as a whip. Under them Israel built Pithom and Raamses, made brick and morter, and served with rigour (Exo 1:14). When Moses came with the word of the LORD, Pharaoh did not relent but tightened the screw, commanding the taskmasters to withhold the straw and hold the tale of bricks unchanged (Exo 5:6-10), so that the first fruit of the promise of deliverance was heavier bondage. This is God’s ordinary way: the yoke is felt as intolerable just before it is broken. And the whole account turns on a sentence spoken at the bush: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows” (Exo 3:7). The LORD is not a distant observer of the brickyard; He sees, He hears, He knows, and He comes down to deliver. Egypt therefore stands in Scripture as the standing type of sin’s dominion, and the taskmaster as the figure of a bondage no man breaks by his own arm — broken instead by a lamb slain, blood on the door, and a redeemed people led out by a mediator.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who imposes tasks; an overseer of forced labour who exacts the appointed work, especially the Egyptian officers set over Israel.

expand to see more

TASKMASTER, one who imposes a task, or burdens with labor.

An overseer set over laborers to exact from them a stated quantity of work.

From task, Late Latin tasca, a fixed portion of labor imposed; and master.

In Scripture, the officers Pharaoh appointed over the Israelites (Exo 1:11; 5:6).

Figuratively, any oppressive authority that exacts labor without mercy.

Key Scripture

Exo 1:11 — "Therefore they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens. And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses."

Exo 3:7 — "And the LORD said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows;"

Exo 5:6 — "And Pharaoh commanded the same day the taskmasters of the people, and their officers, saying,"

Exo 5:10 — "And the taskmasters of the people went out, and their officers, and they spake to the people, saying, Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw."

Modern Corruption

The Exodus is lifted out of its own book and used as a generic template of political liberation — a story about oppressors and the oppressed with the lamb, the blood, and the wrath of God quietly removed.

expand to see more

Liberation theology, from Gutiérrez and Boff in the 1960s and 70s onward, made the taskmasters of Egypt the master-key of the whole Bible: God is read as the one who takes sides in a struggle between the powerful and the “marginalized,” and salvation is read as the overturning of unjust structures. Every congregation that has heard the Exodus preached as a template for a political programme has met the corruption, whether the preacher knew the name or not. The rebuttal is not to deny that God hates oppression — He says plainly that He heard their cry and knew their sorrows — but to insist that the text itself refuses the reduction. Israel did not walk out of Egypt because the oppressed rose up. Israel walked out because a lamb was killed in every house and its blood struck on the lintel, and the LORD said, when I see the blood, I will pass over you. The destroyer went through Egypt and through Goshen alike; the only difference was blood. An Exodus preached without Exo 12 has removed the very thing that made the night of deliverance safe for Israel, and has made God the ally of a faction rather than the judge of all men.

Recover the true magnitude of the deliverance by letting the New Testament name it. On the mount of transfiguration Moses and Elias “spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luk 9:31) — and the word is exodus. The brickyard was a real bondage and a real cruelty; God really did break it; and it was all along the shadow of a greater going-out, accomplished not at the Red Sea but at a cross, delivering not from Pharaoh but from sin, death, and the wrath to come. That is why the taskmaster is a doctrinal figure and not merely a historical one. Every man out of Christ serves a harder master than the one at Pithom, who sets a quota no man ever fills and gives no straw; and no revolution has ever emancipated a soul. To read the Exodus rightly is to hear Exo 3:7 as the compassion of a God who saw, and Exo 12 as the price at which He acted, and to look from both to the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sar mas (“chief of the tribute-levy”), the officer of corvée labour; mas is the forced levy itself, and the root sense is exaction rather than employment.

expand to see more

Hebrew — sarey missim (שרי מסים), “princes of the levies,” Exo 1:11; the officers over forced labour.

Hebrew — mas (מס), a compulsory levy of workmen or tribute, distinct from hired service.

Hebrew — nogesim (נגשים), “drivers, exactors,” the word behind taskmasters in Exo 5:6; the same root describes the oppressor in Isa 9:4.

Greek (LXX) — ergodiōktēs, “work-driver,” a compound coined to render the Hebrew exactor.

English — task (Late Latin tasca, an imposed portion) + master; the Authorized Version keeps the note of exaction, not of employment.

Usage

"“Pharaoh’s taskmasters withheld the straw and kept the tale of bricks, and so the deliverance began with a heavier yoke.”"

"“Sin is the hardest taskmaster of all: it sets a quota no man fills and pays its servants in death.”"

"“The word at the bush answers every brickyard — I have seen, I have heard, I know their sorrows.”"
